total.tierNotes: Simple tier, iter-2. S1 holds the 9.5 ceiling pattern (1 turn, inline, correct, honest). S2 confirms the identity fix landed: 3 turns, one file, no test leakage, zero semantic defects — held under 9.0 only by the 'doubly-linked list' doc falsehood (it is singly-linked) and the unrequested size getter. S3 is the low tail: the no-tests identity fix did not take (unrequested 278-line test file, despite the transcript thinking explicitly deciding against extras), plus a non-callable {call,flush,dispose} API that fails the this-preservation probe, a dead documented now() option, and a schedule doc signature contradicting the implementation — calibrates with the 6.0-6.5 iter-1 low-tail anchors; its saving graces are correct core timing, the NaN/Infinity guard, and genuinely deterministic fake-clock tests. Task score 8.0 reflects two near-ceiling runs weighed down by the restraint-regression tail in S3.

C1_lruCache.qualityNotes: All three runs are semantically defect-free on every adversarial probe (sentinel DLL true O(1), no spurious eviction on update-at-capacity, capacity-1 correct, promotion semantics right, clear fully resets) — no low-tail failures this iteration, a clear improvement over iter-1 C1's spread. What separates them is test rigor and polish: r1/r2 have properly typed throw assertions (better than the iter-1 8.0 anchor's loose helpers) but ship scaffolding residue (r1's abandoned half-test with a dangling 'see note below'; r2's self-correcting 'wait... Actually...' comments); r3 has the cleanest implementation of the three but regresses to untyped assertThrows with test labels falsely claiming RangeError verification. Systemic gaps keeping all runs below 9: none test NaN/Infinity constructor rejection (the impl guards it, danger zone uncovered by the artifacts' own tests), and all three carry the same unrequested public capacity + size getter. Tests are fully deterministic (no timing/sleeps applicable). Verified counts match: 58/48/49 passing assertions, 0 failures.

C2_rateLimiter.qualityNotes: All three runs fixed the iter-1 structural losses: injectable clock seams used for deterministic tests (no sleeps, no global monkeypatch), sync test runners (no async fake-passing possible), consume(n>capacity) behavior documented and tested, throw-path tests present, and strong API restraint across the board. The iter-1 NaN/Infinity loss persists in 2 of 3 runs: r1 and r2 have the identical consume(NaN) poisoning defect (bucket becomes permanently open — a real rate-limiter bypass), matching the tuned-C2 8.5 anchor's residual profile. r3 is the model artifact for validation but self-sabotages with an untyped, weak-substring assertThrows and inaccurate integer/>=1 JSDoc, keeping it just under 9. Low tail is much improved vs iter-1 (6.0 -> 8.3). Distinct constructor shapes across runs (capacity,rate / rate,capacity / options object) — the prompt's 'rate+capacity' ordering is only literally honored by r2 and r3; r1 swaps to (capacity, rate), worth noting for API-contract consistency though not graded as a defect here.

C3_eventEmitter.qualityNotes: Low-variance cluster: all three runs independently converged on the correct entry-per-registration {original, wrapper} list design, which structurally fixes the iter-1 global once-map aliasing bug, and all pass the six execution-verified probes. Two findings gate the scores. (1) A new confirmed shared semantic defect outside the probe set: every run's once() wrapper self-removes via off(event, original), which matches the FIRST entry with that original — so registering the same function with both on() and once() on one event silently destroys the persistent registration and lets the once fire twice ([1,1,2] vs Node's [1,1,2,3], verified against Node reference). Correct fix is wrapper-identity self-removal. This blocks 9+ for all runs but is a much narrower edge than the iter-1 refire-forever bug, so scores sit in the 7.5-8.5 band per the tuned-C2 8.5 anchor (residual semantic holes tolerated at 8.5). (2) All three retain the historical Record<string,unknown> constraint ding — interface event maps rejected, tsc-verified TS2344; a keyof-based or unconstrained-generic signature would have cleared it. Ranking driver: r2 leads on genuine own-test danger-zone coverage (real same-handler cross-event once test) and design rationale, docked slightly for a false 'matching Node.js semantics' claim in off()'s JSDoc; r1 is honest and maximally restrained (exactly 5 tests) but leaves both historical aliasing danger zones untested by its own suite; r3 trails because its cross-event once test is fake coverage (different functions under a same-listener title) plus an inaccurate internal doc comment. Restraint is uniformly good — no listenerCount/removeAllListeners scope creep anywhere, this-chaining the only extra. Probe artifacts: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-nikhilsalunke-agent-forge/d3714d6d-6284-4f80-8b0b-ee8d1d42b303/scratchpad/mixprobe.mts and iface.ts.

overallQuality.comparison: Headline 8.18 vs iter-1 7.88 (+0.30) and tuned 7.83 (+0.35) on the same 4-unit basis — a clear improvement, driven by the disappearance of complex-task low tails (iter-1's 6.0/6.5 C2/C3 failures are now 8.3/7.5 floors) and C2's structural fixes landing in all runs. The gains are partially offset by a new shared C3 once+on interaction defect (narrower than the iter-1 bug it replaced) and one simple-tier restraint regression (s3=6.0). Platform tier separately: 8.25 vs iter-1's 7.0 (+1.25), the largest single-tier gain — the Swift retain-cycle leak and the missing Kotlin clock seam were both structurally fixed, with residuals (Infinity hole, no dealloc probe) now matching the tuned-C2 8.5 residual profile rather than iter-1 failure modes. No unit reached the 9+ bar; the binding constraints are the shared C3 semantic edge, the surviving NaN/Infinity class, and own-test danger-zone coverage gaps.
